summary.text: PageRank is an algorithm Google Search uses to rank web pages, measuring a page's importance by counting the number and quality of links to it.
A hyperlink to a page counts as a vote of support, and a page linked to by many pages with high PageRank receives a high rank itself.
The algorithm outputs a probability distribution representing the likelihood that a person randomly clicking on links will arrive at a particular page.

paragraphs.heading: What it measures
paragraphs.text: PageRank is a link analysis algorithm: it gives each document in a linked collection, such as the World Wide Web, a number meant to measure how important it is within that collection. That number is called the PageRank of the document, written P R (E) for a page E. It is estimated from the number and the quality of the links pointing to a page. The assumption behind it is that more important websites tend to attract more links from other sites. The same method can be applied to any collection of things that quote and refer to each other.

paragraphs.heading: Links as votes
paragraphs.text: Every hyperlink pointing at a page is treated as a vote of support. But a page's PageRank depends both on how many pages link to it and on the PageRank of those pages, so the definition is recursive. A page linked to by many pages with high PageRank ends up with a high rank itself. The calculation runs on the Webgraph, in which every web page is a node and every hyperlink is an edge.

paragraphs.heading: A random clicker
paragraphs.text: There is also a probabilistic way to read the result. PageRank produces a probability distribution that gives, for each page, the likelihood that a person clicking on links at random will arrive there. It works for document collections of any size. Several research papers begin the calculation by sharing the probability out evenly among all the documents.

paragraphs.heading: Born at Stanford
paragraphs.text: In 1996, at Stanford University, Larry Page and Sergey Brin built PageRank, in a research project on a new kind of search engine. Brin's idea was that information on the web could be ordered by link popularity, with a page ranking higher the more links point to it. Their first paper on the project, written with Rajeev Motwani and Terry Winograd and published in 1998, described PageRank and the first prototype of the Google search engine. Shortly after, Page and Brin founded Google Inc. The name plays on Larry Page's surname and on the idea of a web page.

paragraphs.heading: An idea found more than once
paragraphs.text: The eigenvalue problem behind the algorithm was rediscovered independently and reused for many scoring problems. In 1895 Edmund Landau suggested it for deciding the winner of a chess tournament, and in 1976 it was proposed for ranking scientific journals. On the web, Robin Li's RankDex search engine, launched in 1996, ranked sites by how many other sites linked to them. Larry Page cited Li's work in some of his patents for PageRank.

paragraphs.heading: PageRank today
paragraphs.text: PageRank was the first algorithm Google used to order search results and is the best known, though Google does not rely on it alone today. It is one of many factors in Google's rankings, yet it still underlies every one of Google's web-search tools. The patent, granted in 2001, was assigned to Stanford University rather than Google, and Stanford sold the 1.8 million Google shares it received for its use for $336 million in 2005. As of September 24, 2019, all patents linked to PageRank have expired. In practice the idea may be open to manipulation, and researchers have looked for ways to spot falsely influenced rankings.
